explanations: Camelids originated in North America, and the ancestor of the modern animal crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia about six million years ago.
The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world population and the two-humped Bactrian the other 6%.
The wider family, Camelidae, also holds the New World llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña.
As livestock it provides milk, meat, fibre and felt, and it is a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.
It is an even-toed ungulate of the genus Camelus, bearing the fatty deposits known as humps, and suited to desert habitat.

sources.excerpt: Camelids originated in North America during the Eocene, with the ancestor of modern camels, Paracamelus, migrating across the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late Miocene, around 6 million years ago.
The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world's camel population, and the two-humped Bactrian camel makes up 6%.

The word camel is also used informally in a wider sense, where the more correct term is "camelid", to include all seven species of the family Camelidae: the true camels (the above three species), along with the "New World" camelids: the llama, the alpaca, the guanaco, and the vicuña, which belong to the separate tribe Lamini.

Camels have long been domesticated and, as livestock, they provide food (camel milk and meat) and textiles (fiber and felt from camel hair). Camels are working animals especially suited to their desert habitat and are a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.

A camel (from Latin: camelus and Ancient Greek: κάμηλος (kamēlos) from Ancient Semitic: gāmāl) is an even-toed ungulate in the genus Camelus that bears distinctive fatty deposits known as "humps" on its back.
